items.explanation: Inveigh means to attack something verbally with strong and bitter words, so Denounce is the closest synonym: the preacher publicly condemns gambling as a ruin and a theft. items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to INVEIGH as it is used in the sentence: 'The preacher inveighed against gambling from the pulpit, calling it a ruin of families and a theft from the poor.'

items.explanation: Recalcitrant means stubbornly refusing to obey or cooperate, so Defiant is the closest synonym: the committee rejects every compromise and sends the talks back to the start. items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to RECALCITRANT as it is used in the sentence: 'The recalcitrant committee refused every compromise, rejected the mediator's plan outright and sent the talks back to the start.'

items.explanation: The passage traces fast growth from UPI's free, simple design and then turns to the harder problems of the next stage: patchy networks, low literacy, fear of fraud and the habit of cash. options: The government should stop promoting digital payments.

items.passage: In less than a decade, India has moved from a cash-heavy economy to one of the world's most active digital payment markets. The Unified Payments Interface, launched in 2016, now processes more than ten billion transactions a month, a scale no other real-time payment system has reached. A vegetable vendor in a small town and a shopkeeper in a metro city both display the same square QR code, and a customer with any bank account can pay either of them in seconds, free of charge. This simplicity is the core of the system's success. Unlike card networks, which charge merchants a fee on every sale, UPI transfers cost the merchant nothing, so even the smallest seller has a reason to accept them. The government pushed the change further by linking bank accounts to mobile numbers and identity numbers, bringing crores of first-time account holders into the formal financial system. For these new users, a payment app became the first banking service they ever used, and for many it remains the only one. The benefits are visible. Small businesses that once kept all their money in cash now have a record of every sale, and that record helps them borrow from banks at lower rates. Wages that used to be paid in envelopes on a Friday evening now arrive directly into workers' accounts, on time and in full. Street vendors report that digital payments have also cut the risk of carrying cash home late at night, and many now save a part of each day's earnings through the same app that collects their payments. The National Payments Corporation, which runs UPI, has kept the system open so that any bank or app can join it, and that openness is a large part of why adoption spread so quickly. Government subsidies for cooking gas and food reach beneficiaries without passing through layers of middlemen who once took a cut. Yet the shift is far from complete. Surveys show that cash still accounts for a large share of everyday transactions, especially in rural areas where mobile networks are weak and smartphones are shared within families. Trust is another barrier. Stories of fraud, a wrong tap that sends money to a stranger, or a failed transaction that takes days to reverse make cautious users fall back on cash. items.passage: In a cold stone parsonage on the Yorkshire moors, three sisters wrote novels that would outlive them by nearly two centuries. Charlotte, Emily and Anne Bronte lived far from the literary world of London, yet their books reached straight into its heart. When Charlotte's Jane Eyre appeared in 1847, readers were startled by a heroine who was plain, poor and fiercely independent, and who demanded to be loved for her mind rather than her face. In the same year, Emily's Wuthering Heights shocked readers even more with its wild landscapes and its furious, unsentimental love. Anne's quieter novels, Agnes Grey and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, attacked the drinking and cruelty of idle gentlemen with a moral clarity her sisters did not attempt. What made the sisters remarkable was not only what they wrote but how they wrote it. They had spent their childhood inventing imaginary kingdoms, writing tiny hand-sewn books filled with stories of heroes, villains and wars. That private world of invention gave them a freedom that formal education might have taken away, and their novels carry the same intensity of a child's secret game played with adult seriousness. Their isolation mattered too. The moors around Haworth were empty and harsh, and the sisters walked them daily in all weathers. The landscape entered their fiction directly: the wind, the heather, the stone walls and the sudden storms became characters in their own right, shaping the moods of the people who lived among them. Yet the sisters were not cut off from ideas. They read widely, followed the newspapers, and argued about politics and religion at the dinner table. Their novels engage with the great questions of their age: the position of women, the cruelty of the class system, and the right of the individual to judge for herself. Jane Eyre's famous declaration that women feel just as men feel was a direct challenge to a society that expected women to be silent and obedient. The sisters paid a price for their honesty. Critics called their work coarse and unfeminine, and they published under male pen names to be taken seriously. Charlotte wrote as Currer Bell, Emily as Ellis Bell, and Anne as Acton Bell, and the secret of their identity held for years. Their lives were short: Emily died at thirty, Anne at twenty-nine, and Charlotte at thirty-eight, yet in that brief span they changed the English novel for ever. Charlotte lived long enough to see her work praised and to meet the writers she admired, but she outlived both her sisters and mourned them for the rest of her short life. Later writers learned from them that a novel could be built around a woman's inner life, that landscape could carry emotion, and that passion need not be polite to be true. Today the parsonage at Haworth is a museum, and visitors still walk the moors the sisters walked, looking for the places their fiction made famous. The books remain in print in dozens of languages, read by people who have never seen Yorkshire and never will, because the feelings in them belong to no single place or time.

items.passage: For centuries, wetlands were treated as wasteland: damp, mosquito-ridden ground that was useful only when drained and built upon. Cities filled them in for housing, farmers drained them for fields, and engineers straightened the rivers that fed them. Only in recent decades have scientists and planners begun to understand what was lost. A wetland is not empty land waiting for a better use; it is one of the hardest-working ecosystems on the planet, and its services are worth far more than the buildings that replace it. The most valuable service a wetland provides is flood control. Like a sponge, it absorbs rainwater and river overflow, holds it, and releases it slowly. A single hectare of wetland can store thousands of cubic metres of water that would otherwise rush downstream and flood homes and roads. When the city of Chennai was hit by devastating floods in 2015, researchers pointed to the loss of its wetlands as a major cause: the city had paved over the very land that once soaked up the rain. Wetlands also clean water. As water passes slowly through reeds and mud, sediments settle, nutrients are absorbed by plants, and many pollutants break down. Towns that protect their wetlands spend less on water treatment, because nature does part of the work for free. They are also nurseries for life. Fish spawn in the shallow, sheltered waters, birds stop there on long migrations, and a huge variety of plants and insects thrive in the meeting of land and water. Nearly half of the world's threatened species depend on wetlands at some stage of their lives, which makes these habitats far more important than their small share of the earth's surface suggests. Beyond ecology, wetlands support livelihoods. Fisherfolk, reed cutters, and farmers who grow rice in the wet margins all depend on them, and in many parts of Asia and Africa the wetland is the centre of the local economy. Tourism adds another income: birdwatchers and nature lovers travel long distances to visit famous wetlands, bringing money to nearby villages. Despite all this, wetlands are disappearing three times faster than forests. The Ramsar Convention, an international treaty signed in 1971, now lists more than two thousand wetlands of international importance, but listing alone does not protect them. Enforcement is weak, and the pressure to drain land for agriculture and construction remains strong in fast-growing countries. Climate change makes the loss more dangerous. As rainfall becomes heavier and less predictable, the flood-absorbing capacity of wetlands matters more, not less. At the same time, rising seas threaten coastal wetlands with salt water, and hotter summers dry out inland marshes. The answer is not to fence off every wetland but to manage them wisely: restore the ones that have been damaged, keep new construction away from the most sensitive areas, and pay local people for protecting them rather than for draining them. Some cities have begun to do this, turning old wetlands into parks that absorb floods and give residents green space at the same time. The lesson is simple: a wetland is not a waste of land, it is a piece of infrastructure, and like any infrastructure it works best when it is maintained.

items.passage: When Eleanor Roosevelt arrived at the United Nations in 1946, few expected her to achieve much. She had been the First Lady of the United States, but she had never held elected office, and the diplomats around the table were mostly men who doubted that a widow in her sixties could lead them. Within two years she had proved them wrong by guiding the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, a document that still shapes the way the world talks about freedom and dignity. Roosevelt's strength was not legal scholarship but persistence and common sense. She chaired a committee of eighteen people from different countries, cultures and political systems, and she kept them working through disagreements that often seemed impossible to resolve. When the Soviet delegates insisted that economic rights mattered more than political freedoms, and the Western delegates argued the opposite, she found language that allowed both sides to sign. She worked late into the night, read every draft herself, and refused to let the committee adjourn until the text was finished. Her approach to human rights was practical rather than abstract. She had visited slums and coal mines, met refugees and soldiers, and she believed that rights meant little unless they changed daily life. The Declaration she helped write therefore speaks of food, housing, education and work alongside freedom of speech and belief, because she knew that a hungry person cannot enjoy liberty. After the Declaration was adopted in December 1948, Roosevelt continued to fight for it, travelling the world to explain it and defending it against those who called it unrealistic. She once said that human rights begin in small places, close to home: in the neighbourhood, the school, the factory and the farm. Roosevelt's own life had taught her what hardship meant. Orphaned before she was ten, she was raised by a strict grandmother and sent to school in England, where a French headmistress, Marie Souvestre, encouraged her to think for herself and to care about the poor. Those years shaped the reformer she became, and she never forgot the loneliness of her childhood or the kindness of the teacher who believed in her. After the White House years she did not retire. She wrote a daily newspaper column, My Day, for more than twenty-five years, answering readers' letters and reporting on the places she visited. She supported the civil rights movement in America, resigned from organisations that refused black members, and used her fame to give a hearing to people who had none. In her seventies she was still travelling, still chairing committees, and still insisting that the work of rights was never finished. Unless rights have meaning there, she argued, they have little meaning anywhere. That belief guided everything she did, from the committee room in New York to the villages she visited on her travels. Her legacy is not only the document itself but the idea that ordinary people, not only lawyers and diplomats, own the language of rights and can use it to demand better lives.

items.explanation: Factorise 1155: its factors are 1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 15, 21, 33, 35, 55, 77, 105, 165, 231, 385, 1155. Since 1155 is odd, a + b is odd, so one of the primes is 2, and since a < b, a is 2. Then b is a factor minus 2, and each candidate must be prime and below 150, which leaves 7 values: 3, 5, 13, 19, 31, 53, 103. Missing a candidate or keeping a composite one changes the count by one or two.

items.explanation: Let the prime factorisation of N have exponents e1, e2, and so on. Then N has (e1+1)(e2+1)... = 12 divisors, and N squared has (2e1+1)(2e2+1)... = 45 divisors. Every factor in the second product is odd and greater than 1, so 45 must split as 45, or 15 x 3, or 9 x 5, or 5 x 3 x 3, giving exponent patterns 22, 7 and 1, 4 and 2, and 2, 1 and 1. Four odd factors are impossible, since 3 x 3 x 3 x 3 = 81 is already greater than 45. Only the pattern 2, 1 and 1 gives a divisor count of 3 x 2 x 2 = 12, so N is a squared prime times two distinct primes. Since N is divisible by 6, the primes 2 and 3 both divide N, and 5 does not. To make N as small as possible, put the exponent 2 on the smallest prime, 2, and use the smallest available primes for the other two factors, 3 and 7, giving N = 4 x 3 x 7 = 84. The option 60 is 2^2 x 3 x 5, which satisfies both divisor counts but is divisible by 5; 72 is 2^3 x 3^2, whose square has 7 x 5 = 35 divisors; 96 is 2^5 x 3, whose square has 11 x 3 = 33 divisors; and 126 is 2 x 3^2 x 7, which satisfies every condition but is larger than 84.

items.question: By what percentage is the highest value more than the lowest value, after the lowest value is revised up by 10%?

items.explanation: The year-on-year changes are +25% in 2020, -28% in 2021, +66.7% in 2022 and +16.7% in 2023, and their average is about 20.1%. The profit rose from 20 to 35 over four years, so the compound annual growth rate is the fourth root of 35/20 minus 1, about 15.0%. The average of the yearly percentage changes is therefore greater than the compound rate. The compound rate is below 20%, the average is above 15%, and the average yearly absolute change divided by the 2019 figure is 3.75/20, or 18.75%, which is not the compound rate.
